value.overview: The Spot-breasted Oriole (Icterus pectoralis) is a brightly colored oriole of dry and seasonally dry habitats on the Pacific side of Mexico and Central America. It is named for the distinct black spotting across its orange-yellow breast and belly. This active, vocal songbird often lives near people, using flowering trees, fruiting plants, woodland edges, and open country as well as more natural tropical forest habitats.
value.classification: The Spot-breasted Oriole belongs to the oriole family, Icteridae, within the songbird order Passeriformes. It is closely related to other New World orioles in the genus Icterus.
value.identification: Adults have a mainly orange-yellow head and underparts, a black back and wings, and conspicuous white wing bars. The breast and upper belly show bold black spots, while the tail is dark with pale edges. The bill is pointed and slightly curved. Females and immature birds are generally duller and less strongly marked, but they retain the species’ overall orange-yellow, black, and white pattern. Its clear, varied whistles and chatter often reveal it before it is seen.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs along the Pacific slope from western and southern Mexico through Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, and into Costa Rica. In Costa Rica it is primarily associated with the Pacific lowlands and foothills, especially seasonally dry areas such as Guanacaste and the northwestern lowlands, and may also occur locally in cultivated landscapes and towns. Typical habitats include tropical dry forest, scrub, woodland edges, savanna-like areas, plantations, gardens, and other open habitats with scattered trees.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident or locally nomadic rather than a long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, it is expected mainly as a year-round species in suitable Pacific lowland habitats, with local movements possible as food and water conditions change.
value.breeding: Breeding generally takes place during the local wet-season period, when food and nesting materials become more available. The female builds a hanging, woven nest from plant fibers, usually suspended from a branch in a tree or shrub. A clutch commonly contains several eggs, which the female incubates. Both adults feed the nestlings. Timing and nesting success vary geographically, and detailed information is better documented in some parts of the range than in Costa Rica.
value.dietFeeding: The Spot-breasted Oriole eats a mixed diet of insects, other small arthropods, fruit, nectar, and occasionally small vertebrate or other animal food. It searches among foliage and branches, probes flowers, and takes fruit from trees and shrubs. In Costa Rica, it may forage in dry forest, gardens, plantations, and wooded urban areas, where flowering and fruiting plants can provide important food during seasonal changes in availability.
value.behavior: This oriole is active and conspicuous, often moving through the middle and upper levels of trees while calling frequently. It may forage alone, in pairs, or in small groups, and can join mixed feeding flocks outside the breeding season. Adults defend nesting areas but may tolerate nearby orioles where food is abundant. Its ability to use altered habitats makes it a familiar bird around farms, gardens, and settlements in parts of its range.

conservation.populationTrend: The species is not currently considered globally threatened, although its population trend is not precisely quantified across its entire range.
